components.text: Whether the proposed late dates establish provenance too remote or uninformed to support historical trust.
Whether anonymous composition and a lengthy oral chain are the best explanation of the written Gospels.
Whether the proposed late chronology leaves the Gospels without sufficiently informed provenance.
Whether years of oral and cross-language transmission sever the accounts from informed early sources.
Whether prediction of Jerusalem's fall independently requires dating the relevant Gospel material after 70.
Whether Jerusalem's predicted fall requires dating the Gospel account after the year 70.
Whether Luke's author had demonstrable access to Jesus's disciples or another specifically informed source.
Whether Palestinian linguistic and contextual features could remain present after a long cross-language oral transmission.
Whether cross-language oral transmission could preserve wording and integrated Palestinian contextual knowledge.
Whether Luke's contents provide internal evidence of access to early Palestinian material.
Whether later composition is better explained by invention than by preserved early tradition.
Whether accurate and integrated Palestinian setting details warrant the truth of the central reported sayings and events.
Whether accurate Palestinian setting information warrants the historical truth of the central Jesus narratives.
Whether preservation of numerous incidental Palestinian details is best explained by preservation of the main tradition.
Whether clusters of accurate Palestinian details establish that the substantive tradition was preserved.
Whether the observed Palestinian details could plausibly survive many stages while the main traditions underwent substantial change.
Whether accurate name patterns directly establish the truth of the central reported events.
Whether accurate incidental details can persist despite many stages of substantially altering oral transmission.
Whether contextual evidence has probabilistic force beyond merely accurate scenery.
Whether the oral transmission chain was long enough to predict corruption of local names.
Whether hanging and falling headlong necessarily describe incompatible manners of Judas's death.
Whether the two accounts' purchaser, sequence, and explanation of the field's name are jointly reconcilable.
The decisive alleged incompatibility is answered by treating Matthew's hanging as the omitted elevation that could precede Acts' headlong fall and rupture.
Whether the proposed hanging-then-fall reconstruction resolves the specific Judas narratives on textual evidence.
The earlier move must show that its proposed Judas sequence is supported by historical evidence, not merely available because theological commitments favor reconciliation.
Whether contextual Palestinian knowledge warrants preserved tradition and broader historical reliability across the four Gospels.
The earlier Judas reconstruction requires textual support for its causal sequence, whereas this move instead advances a separate chronology-based case about Jesus' changing portrait.
Whether a low earlier portrait followed by John's exalted portrait supports a simple late-development sequence.
The development inference must account for Mark's already exalted portrait of Jesus through scriptural allusions, forgiveness, miracles, and actions associated with God.
Whether an exalted narrator's portrait in Mark answers the absence of explicit Johannine-style self-claims in earlier sources.
Mark's narrator portraying Jesus as divine does not answer the distributional demand concerning whether earlier sources report Jesus explicitly making John's divine self-claims.
Whether Johannine first-person identity sayings lack meaningful precedent in the earlier Synoptic traditions.
The decisive absence claim is answered by identifying conceptual precedents for Johannine self-descriptions in Synoptic sayings and narrative roles despite unequal wording and coverage.
Selective Gospel coverage and Synoptic conceptual precedents provide a rival explanation to a simple progression from kingdom proclamation to invented divine identity.
Whether oral transmission plausibly preserved incidental context while substantially altering distinctive central traditions.
Whether traditions unique to later or individual Gospels reflect development rather than genuine preservation.
The claim that contextual accuracy can coexist with alteration is answered by adding literary integrity, scriptural depth, and Palestinian Jewish fit as convergent evidence of genuine preservation.
The oral-transmission gap is answered in part by arguing that distinctive traditions exhibit internal and contextual features more expected under early preservation.
Whether historical conclusions should remain governed by evidence rather than predetermined theological requirements.
Whether the proposed dating and development of miraculous or exalted traditions may reflect naturalistic assumptions.
An evidence-first method fails its own standard if naturalistic assumptions automatically classify miraculous sayings or stories as late before their particular evidence is assessed.
Whether naturalistic assumptions actually cause scholars to classify miraculous Gospel traditions as late by default.
The bias charge does not establish dogmatic exclusion when historical study is undertaken to determine what is right with an open willingness to revise foundational beliefs.
